title: Check records sooner, inquest jury says
article: Police should be doing checks as soon as possible to learn everything they can about a suspect, a coroner's jury in Prince Albert is recommending.
The suggestion, which is not binding, arose from an examination of the death of Jacqueline Montgrand, 44, who was shot by police in Prince Albert, Sask., in 2008.
Police were at her home to enforce an eviction notice when Montgrand, who was very drunk, turned suddenly violent and threatened officers with a steak knife.
She was ordered to stop, but did not. She was shot four times by officers and died.
The coroner's jury said Friday that police should go to their database, known as CPIC, at the earliest opportunity.
In the Montgrand case, officers on the scene were told by their dispatcher that the woman was noted in the CPIC system as potentially violent.
That information, however, was conveyed only seconds before the shooting.
Family members of the dead woman said Friday they believe that had officers known, sooner, about the risk of violence they might have approached the eviction differently.
"She could have been [behind] bars right now, rather than dead," Myrna Laprise, a niece of Montgrand, said. "It could have been maybe a different outcome than this situation, if a CPIC was done."
During the inquest, officers testified they didn't perform a CPIC check because they thought they would be dealing with a routine eviction call.
That may change, according to the lawyer who represented the police department.
"The recommendation will be considered," Mitch Holash said. "The Prince Albert Police Service will take it ... to its operations meetings and determine whether it's practical."
Family members said they are considering a wrongful death lawsuit, against the Prince Albert police.
